sections.html:
A Dayton seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash purchase. Whichever route you pick, the sale runs through a city disclosure step that most Ohio cities don't have. Dayton is the Montgomery County seat, and the population is 136,688 for July 2025, down slightly from 137,644 in 2020. It is the sixth-most populous city in Ohio.

Housing here is inexpensive and mostly rented. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $100,600, and 48.4 percent of households own, so just over half rent. Median gross rent is $918, and median monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $1,147. With that many renters, plenty of Dayton houses are sold by landlords with tenants still inside, and many others come out of estates. Both situations are covered below.

Population peaked at 262,332 in 1960, so many blocks were built for a city far larger than today's. Buyers know it, and they look hard at roof age, windows and past repairs, especially in the older historic neighborhoods such as Oregon District, Dayton View, Grafton Hill and South Park. If you own in one of those areas, collect repair invoices before you list.

sections.h2: The City of Dayton Certificate of Disclosure
sections.html:
Any sale of a property inside the city requires a Certificate of Disclosure that tells the buyer about open housing code violations. Look at the parcel number: if it starts with R72 or R726, the property is in Dayton and the form must be filed. The form exists to inform the buyer. It isn't meant to stop a sale.

  • With no open violations, the seller signs and supplies the buyer's contact details.
  • With open violations, the form must show the violation or structural nuisance status, a flat $60 fee is paid (not per violation), and both parties sign, with the buyer's signature notarized.
  • The buyer agrees either that the violations are corrected before the sale or that the buyer will make the listed repairs within 90 days.
  • The title company usually asks the city for violation information and pending bills 7 to 10 business days before closing.

Selling doesn't remove violations. They transfer with the house, which is why the buyer has to sign on to the repairs. The city's FAQ lists exceptions for three types of transfer, so ask the city whether yours is one of them.

The Division of Housing and Inspections enforces the housing ordinance and the public nuisance ordinance. Its work also covers trees and trash, non-residential exterior maintenance, and abandoned or junk vehicles. For an open violation notice or citation, call 937-333-3867 or 937-333-8645.

Two online tools let you see what a buyer can see. The Dayton Housing Tracker searches by address or neighborhood, and the Dayton Housing Condition Survey portal shows housing conditions by neighborhood. Complaints and service requests go through Dayton Delivers.

Look up your own address before you list. If a citation is on file, you can fix it, price around it, or plan the disclosure form with the buyer. Finding it early is far cheaper than finding it when the title company calls the city a week or two before closing.

sections.h2: Storm history and the Ohio condition form
sections.html:
Dayton has hot, humid summers and cold winters, and severe thunderstorms, floods, blizzards and tornadoes are all possible. On Memorial Day 2019, a tornado outbreak put 15 tornadoes on the ground in the Dayton area, including an EF4 that tore through Brookville, Trotwood, Dayton, Northridge and Riverside.

Roofs, siding and basements are where buyers look for storm history. Keep repair invoices, insurance claim paperwork and contractor names in one folder. That lets you answer the state disclosure form with documents instead of memory, and it shortens the back and forth after an inspection.

A landlord selling a rental should check city permit rules, tenant protections and short-term use before setting a price. Dayton requires a contractor registered with the city for plumbing, electrical and HVAC work on rental property, on an unoccupied house that will be rented, and on duplexes, even where the owner lives in one half. Owner-occupants may do some of that work themselves after getting the right permits.

The city's FAQ also describes source of income rules: landlords can't refuse a prospective tenant because rent comes from vouchers, subsidies, benefits or other public assistance. A sale doesn't end a lease, so read it for the end date and notice terms and tell buyers early.

Short-term rentals are stays under 30 consecutive days. The city has no registration system for them and handles concerns case by case. If your buyer plans to use the house that way, ask the city planning office what applies before you sign.

The Montgomery County Auditor handles the deed transfer, and the Recorder records the deed afterward.

Montgomery County deed transfer and recording rates
StepRate
Conveyance fee$3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price
Per parcel$.50 for each parcel transferred
Recording a deed$34 for the first two pages, $8 per additional page
Payment to the RecorderCash, check or money order to the Montgomery County Recorder

The deed goes to the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department for a transfer stamp before it reaches the Recorder. Questions go to the deed transfer line at 937-225-4373. Electronic filing is available through two named e-recording services, and most sellers let the title company handle it.

sections.h2: What Ohio law adds to the city form
sections.html:
State law (R.C. 5302.30) has the seller of a one-to-four-unit home fill out Ohio's own condition form and deliver a signed copy. If the buyer sees it only after a contract is signed, a written cancellation is allowed for three business days after receipt, ending no later than thirty days from acceptance or closing, whichever is first.

The state form doesn't replace Dayton's certificate. You need both. The city's certificate concerns open code violations, while the state form covers physical condition items such as the roof, basement and plumbing. Hand over the state form early, at the listing stage, so a late delivery can't give the buyer a way out of the contract.

sections.h2: A step by step plan for a Dayton sale
sections.html:
Start by checking the parcel number so you know the city certificate applies. Look up your address on the Dayton Housing Tracker, then call Housing and Inspections about anything open. Next, gather the paperwork a buyer or title company will ask for: repair invoices, insurance claims, any lease, and the state condition form.

Once you have a contract, the title company requests violation information and pending bills from the city, usually 7 to 10 business days before closing. Expect the deed to go through the Auditor for the transfer stamp and then to the Recorder. Costs at the county level are the conveyance fee, the per-parcel charge and the recording fee in the table above.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, so the timeline is often shorter. That helps with an estate, a tenant-occupied house or a property with open violations. The city certificate and the state form still apply, so ask every buyer to put the price, the closing date and who pays each cost in writing, then compare offers side by side.

faqs.q: How do I know if my Dayton property needs the city disclosure?
faqs.a: Check the parcel number. A number beginning with R72 or R726 is inside the City of Dayton and requires a Certificate of Disclosure. The city's FAQ lists exceptions for three types of transfer.

faqs.q: What does an open violation cost me at sale?
faqs.a: The city charges a flat $60 fee with the disclosure form when there is an open violation, not a per-violation fee. The buyer must also sign before a notary and agree to corrections within 90 days or earlier repairs.

faqs.q: Does selling a Dayton house clear its code violations?
faqs.a: No. A sale doesn't remove violations from a property. They pass to the buyer, who agrees to resolve them.

faqs.q: What is the Montgomery County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The county charges a mandatory conveyance fee of $3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price, plus $.50 for each parcel transferred.
The city has no system to register or regulate short-term rentals and handles concerns case by case. A short-term rental is a stay of less than 30 consecutive days.
